opus-5.5.text:
Honestly? Not very. I think the default state of security at the AI labs is roughly what you'd expect from a startup, and that's just wildly mismatched with what's actually at stake.

The way I'd put it is this: the labs are developing what I think will be the most important national security technology of the century, and they're protecting it like it's a random SaaS product. The relevant threat actors here aren't some hacker in a basement. It's state intelligence services, the Chinese Ministry of State Security and others, who have enormous resources, thousands of people, and decades of experience at exactly this kind of thing. Against that level of adversary, I think current lab security is basically nothing. You can probably walk out with the key algorithmic secrets fairly easily. There are people talking about this stuff at San Francisco parties, there are lots of employees with access, and the vetting is nothing like what you'd see in a classified program.

And I think people underrate the algorithmic secrets in particular. Everyone focuses on the weights, and the weights matter enormously later on. But right now the key insights about how to get past the data wall, how to do RL on top of these models, the next paradigm, those are being developed right now. If those leak, you've essentially handed away a lead that could be worth years. All the export controls on chips don't matter much if you just give away the recipe.

So what would it take? Getting to real security against state-level actors is hard. It means things like air-gapped data centers, security clearances, real compartmentalization, the kind of measures you see around the most sensitive government programs. No single private company can really do that on its own, and there's a competitive cost to doing it unilaterally. That's partly why I think, eventually, government has to be much more involved. But the thing that worries me is that we need to start now. Security takes years to build up, and if we wait until it's obvious to everyone that this matters, the important secrets will already be gone.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, not very. I think this is one of the most underrated issues right now. If you look at the security at the labs today, it's basically the security of a startup. It's not fundamentally different from any random tech company in San Francisco. And that's fine if what you're protecting is a consumer app. It is not fine if what you're protecting is going to be the most important national security asset the United States has in a few years.

The thing people miss is that there are really two things to protect. There are the model weights, which everyone talks about, and then there are the algorithmic secrets. And I'd argue the algorithmic secrets are actually the more pressing problem right now. The weights of GPT-4 or whatever, that's a big file, you can at least imagine locking it down. But the algorithmic insights, the key architectural tricks, the data recipes, the things that get you the next few orders of magnitude of effective compute, those live in people's heads, they're in Slack, they're in Google Docs, they're in code repos that thousands of people can access. And right now those are basically completely unprotected.

And the stakes here are enormous. If China can't match us on compute because of export controls, the way they catch up is by stealing the algorithms. A key algorithmic breakthrough can be worth a 10x or 100x in effective compute. That's the equivalent of billions of dollars of chips, and it's just sitting on a server that a state actor could get at with relatively little effort. We're not talking about a criminal group here. We're talking about the Chinese intelligence services, which have penetrated major defense contractors, government agencies, the Office of Personnel Management. Against that level of adversary, a lab doing a bit better than a normal tech company is basically zero.

So I think what we're doing right now is effectively handing over AGI research to the CCP on a silver platter. Every month that goes by with this stuff unprotected is a month where those secrets could just be leaking out. And the labs will tell you they're working on it, they take it seriously, but the gap between where they are and what you'd need, something like actual government-grade security, airgapped clusters, real vetting, SCIFs for the key research, is enormous. It takes years to build that kind of infrastructure, and we're not even really starting.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re much less secure than they need to be, especially against a determined state actor. There’s a big difference between keeping an ordinary hacker out and protecting something that a major intelligence service considers a strategic priority.

And it’s not just the model weights. It’s the code, the experimental results, the techniques that didn’t work. If someone can read your internal research, they can potentially save themselves an enormous amount of time and compute. You’ve paid to discover which paths are promising, and they get to follow those paths.

I don’t have visibility into every lab’s defenses, so I wouldn’t claim that any particular system has been compromised. But I think the appropriate standard is closer to protecting a national-security secret than protecting a typical technology company’s intellectual property. As these systems become more capable, that gap becomes increasingly consequential.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re much less secure than they need to be. There’s a big difference between protecting yourself against somebody trying to compromise an employee’s account and protecting yourself against a determined state intelligence service.

And the thing you’re protecting isn’t just the model weights. It’s the research: which experiments worked, which approaches failed, the techniques that let you get more capability out of a given amount of compute. If someone can steal those discoveries, they can potentially save themselves an enormous amount of time and money.

I don’t have visibility into every lab’s internal security, so I wouldn’t claim to know exactly who could steal what today. But I think we should be treating frontier AI research as a national-security target. That requires a very different security posture from the one you’d adopt as a normal technology startup.
